# <em>Accessibility</em> {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: common
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

#| label: co_box_rev

How do we reach RStudio Server, JupyterHub, and `baseball-trajectory` on the same instance without opening a port for each one? The answer from [Lab 12](lab12.qmd) is a proxy. In this chapter we install the two new services, keep every port but `80` closed to the outside, and put `nginx` in front. RStudio Server lives at `/rstudio`, JupyterHub at `/jupyter`, and the app from [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd) at `/trajectory`.

## What we're building

Only port `80` opens in the security group. `nginx` listens there and reads the path of each request. It forwards `/rstudio/` to RStudio Server on `8787`, `/jupyter/` to JupyterHub on `8001`, and `/trajectory/` to the app on `8000`. Everything else gets the `nginx` welcome page:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: 'One Port, Four Destinations'
%%| fig-width: 7.0
%%| fig-align: 'center'
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%%

flowchart TD
    Browser(["<strong>Browser</strong>"])
    SG{"Security group<br/><em>port 80 from our IP</em>"}
    subgraph Instance["<strong>EC2 instance</strong>"]
        Nginx("<strong>nginx</strong><br/>:80")
        Welcome("Welcome page<br/><code>/</code>")
        RS("<strong>RStudio Server</strong><br/>127.0.0.1:8787")
        JH("<strong>JupyterHub</strong><br/>127.0.0.1:8001")
        App("<strong>baseball-trajectory</strong><br/>127.0.0.1:8000")
    end

    Browser --> SG --> Nginx
    Nginx --"<code>/</code>"--> Welcome
    Nginx --"<code>/rstudio/</code>"--> RS
    Nginx --"<code>/jupyter/</code>"--> JH
    Nginx --"<code>/trajectory/</code>"--> App

    style Browser fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000
    style SG fill:#D2562B,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff
    style Nginx fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff
    style Welcome fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff
    style RS fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff
    style JH fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff
    style App fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff
```

`baseball-trajectory` already holds `8000`, and JupyterHub uses `8000` by default. JupyterHub moves to `8001` so both can run. In [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd#viewing-the-app) only we could see the app, through an SSH tunnel; here anyone the security group allows can reach it. [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd) later moves it to `443`.

## Logging into the instance

We use the same AL2023 instance from [Instance Size](instance-size.qmd). It already has R 4.6.1 (from `rig`) and Python 3.12.1 in `/opt`. Start it, look up the new IP, and connect the same way as in [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd#logging-into-the-instance), or with `awsdev` from [SSH config](ssh-config.qmd).

The instance is a `t3.small`, which we kept for this chapter (see [Staying on a `t3.small`](instance-size.qmd#staying-on-a-t3.small)). RStudio Server and JupyterHub add two more services that need memory, so check what's free before we start:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
free -h
```

<!-- OUTPUT: free -h -->

## A user to log in with

RStudio Server and JupyterHub both log users in with their Linux username and password. `ec2-user` has no password (we log in with a key), so create a user for the lab and give it one:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo useradd -m datasci
sudo passwd datasci
```

<!-- OUTPUT: sudo passwd datasci (no password shown) -->

`-m` creates `/home/datasci`, which both services need for the user's files and sessions.

## Installing RStudio Server

Posit doesn't build RStudio Server for Amazon Linux. We use the RHEL 9 package, for the same reason `rig` could use the RHEL 9 build of R: AL2023 is close enough to RHEL 9. Copy the current RHEL 9 download link from the [RStudio Server download page](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-server/) and download it:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
cd /tmp
curl -LO https://download2.rstudio.org/server/rhel9/x86_64/rstudio-server-rhel-VERSION-x86_64.rpm
```

<!-- TODO: replace VERSION with the version downloaded -->

`dnf` installs the package and the libraries it depends on:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo dnf install -y ./rstudio-server-rhel-VERSION-x86_64.rpm
```

<!-- OUTPUT: last lines of the dnf install (ending in Complete!) -->

The package installs a `systemd` unit and starts it. Check that it's running:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo systemctl status rstudio-server
```

<!-- OUTPUT: systemctl status rstudio-server (first 5 lines) -->

### Keeping RStudio Server private

RStudio Server listens on every address by default. We want it reachable only through `nginx`, the same way `baseball-trajectory` binds to `127.0.0.1`. Open its config file:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo vim /etc/rstudio/rserver.conf
```

Add one line:

```{verbatim}
www-address=127.0.0.1
```

Restart RStudio Server to load the change:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo systemctl restart rstudio-server
```

We could also set `www-root-path=/rstudio` here. We don't need to, because `nginx` sends the same information in a header (see below).

## Installing JupyterHub

JupyterHub has two parts. The hub logs users in and starts a notebook server for each one. `configurable-http-proxy`, a Node.js program, sits in front and routes each user's traffic to their server. That means JupyterHub needs Node.js as well as Python:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo dnf install -y nodejs npm
sudo npm install -g configurable-http-proxy
```

<!-- OUTPUT: npm install output (last lines) -->

`npm install -g` puts the proxy in `/usr/local/bin`. Check that it's on the `PATH`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
which configurable-http-proxy
```

<!-- OUTPUT: which configurable-http-proxy -->

The Python side gets its own virtual environment in `/opt`, built from the `/opt` Python just like `baseball-trajectory`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo /opt/python/3.12.1/bin/python3.12 -m venv /opt/jupyterhub/.venv
sudo /opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin/pip install jupyterhub jupyterlab
```

<!-- OUTPUT: pip install output (Successfully installed ... line, trimmed) -->

### Configuring JupyterHub

JupyterHub writes a default config file that lists every setting, all commented out. Generate it in `/etc/jupyterhub`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo mkdir -p /etc/jupyterhub
cd /etc/jupyterhub
sudo /opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin/jupyterhub --generate-config
```

<!-- OUTPUT: --generate-config output -->

Open the file and add three settings at the top:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo vim /etc/jupyterhub/jupyterhub_config.py
```

```{verbatim}
c.JupyterHub.bind_url = 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/jupyter' #<1>
c.Spawner.cmd = ['/opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin/jupyterhub-singleuser'] #<2>
c.Spawner.default_url = '/lab' #<3>
```

1. The address, port, and path JupyterHub serves from. `127.0.0.1` keeps it private, `8001` avoids `baseball-trajectory`, and `/jupyter` matches the path in `nginx`.
2. The program that starts each user's notebook server, with its full path into the venv.
3. Users land in JupyterLab instead of the classic notebook page.

The path in `bind_url` is the setting the chapter warns about. JupyterHub writes its links relative to that path. Without `/jupyter`, the login page loads but every link on it points at `/` and gets the `nginx` welcome page instead.

### Running JupyterHub as a service

JupyterHub doesn't ship a unit file, so we write one, the same way we did for `baseball-trajectory` in [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd#the-unit-file):

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo vim /etc/systemd/system/jupyterhub.service
```

```{verbatim}
[Unit]
Description=JupyterHub
After=network.target

[Service]
User=root #<1>
Environment="PATH=/opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin" #<2>
WorkingDirectory=/etc/jupyterhub #<3>
ExecStart=/opt/jupyterhub/.venv/bin/jupyterhub -f /etc/jupyterhub/jupyterhub_config.py
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

1. The hub runs as `root` because it has to start each user's server as that user. This is the opposite of `baseball-trajectory`, which runs as its own service account.
2. The `PATH` has to include `/usr/local/bin`, or the hub can't find `configurable-http-proxy`.
3. The hub writes its cookie secret and user database here.

Load the unit, then enable and start it:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now jupyterhub
sudo systemctl status jupyterhub
```

<!-- OUTPUT: systemctl status jupyterhub (first 10 lines) -->

## Configuring nginx

AL2023's `nginx` package already has a `server` block for port `80` in `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf`. It serves the welcome page, and it reads any file in `/etc/nginx/default.d/`. That means we don't have to replace `nginx.conf`, as the chapter does on Ubuntu. We add two small files instead. Install `nginx` first:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo dnf install -y nginx
```

<!-- OUTPUT: dnf install nginx (last lines) -->

Confirm the default `server` block includes `default.d`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
grep -n 'listen\|default.d' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
```

<!-- OUTPUT: grep listen/default.d -->

### The WebSocket map

RStudio and JupyterLab both keep a WebSocket open to the browser (see [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd)). `nginx` only passes it through when the request asks for an upgrade. A `map` sets that header for us, and it has to live in the `http` block, which reads every file in `conf.d/`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo vim /etc/nginx/conf.d/websocket.conf
```

```{verbatim}
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}
```

### The three locations

The `location` blocks go in `default.d/`, so they join the existing port `80` server:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo vim /etc/nginx/default.d/lab12.conf
```

```{verbatim}
location /rstudio/ {
    rewrite ^/rstudio/(.*)$ /$1 break; #<1>
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8787;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
    proxy_read_timeout 20d; #<2>
    proxy_set_header X-RStudio-Root-Path /rstudio; #<3>
    proxy_set_header Host $host:$server_port;
}

location /jupyter/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8001; #<4>
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
}

location /trajectory/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000/; #<5>
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
}
```

1. RStudio Server expects paths that start at `/`, so `nginx` strips `/rstudio` before passing the request on.
2. Keeps an idle RStudio session's connection open instead of dropping it after 60 seconds.
3. Tells RStudio Server it lives at `/rstudio`, so the links it writes include the prefix.
4. No `rewrite` here. JupyterHub already serves from `/jupyter` (its `bind_url`), so the path passes through unchanged.
5. The trailing `/` on `proxy_pass` strips `/trajectory/` before the request reaches the app. The app thinks it lives at `/`, and it works because Shiny writes its links relative to the page.

Each service handles the path its own way. RStudio Server gets the prefix stripped and a header telling it where it lives. JupyterHub keeps the prefix because its own config already expects it. `baseball-trajectory` gets the prefix stripped and needs nothing else, so its unit file stays as it is.

### Testing and starting nginx

`nginx -t` checks every file for errors before we start the server:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo nginx -t
```

<!-- OUTPUT: sudo nginx -t (syntax is ok / test is successful) -->

Enable and start `nginx`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
```

`ss` shows every service and the address it listens on. Only `nginx` should listen on all addresses (`0.0.0.0:80`); the rest stay on `127.0.0.1`:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
sudo ss -tlnp
```

<!-- OUTPUT: sudo ss -tlnp (expect nginx :80, rserver :8787, configurable-http-proxy :8001, jupyterhub :8081, shiny :8000, sshd :22) -->

Before touching the security group, test all three paths from the instance itself. `curl -I` asks for the headers only:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
curl -I http://127.0.0.1/rstudio/
curl -I http://127.0.0.1/jupyter/
curl -I http://127.0.0.1/trajectory/
```

<!-- OUTPUT: all three curl -I responses (status line and Location header) -->

A `302` is a good sign for the first two. RStudio Server and JupyterHub redirect a visitor who isn't logged in to their sign in page. The app has no login, so it should answer `200 OK`, the same as the `curl -I` in [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd).

## Opening port 80

From outside, the request still hangs. The security group only allows port `22`. Add a rule for port `80` from our local machine:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
  --group-name dev-sg \
  --protocol tcp --port 80 \
  --cidr YOUR_IP/32 \
  --profile dev-deploy
```

<!-- OUTPUT: authorize-security-group-ingress JSON (Return: true) -->

The chapter opens port `80` to everyone (`0.0.0.0/0`). We limit it to our own IP, the same as the SSH rule. This site is plain HTTP, so the `datasci` password crosses the internet unencrypted until [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd) adds HTTPS.

## Trying it out

Open `http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS/` in a browser. The `nginx` welcome page confirms the proxy and the security group work. Then try each path:

* `http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS/rstudio/`: RStudio Server's sign in page. Sign in as `datasci`.
* `http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS/jupyter/`: JupyterHub's login page. Sign in as `datasci`, and JupyterLab opens.
* `http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP_ADDRESS/trajectory/`: `baseball-trajectory`, with no SSH tunnel this time.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: RStudio at /rstudio/, JupyterLab at /jupyter/, and the app at /trajectory/ -->

Type `http://` in full. Some browsers try `https://` first, and nothing listens on `443` yet. Keep the trailing `/` too, since each `location` block matches a path that ends in `/`.

With both sessions open, check memory again:

```{bash}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
#| echo: true
free -h
```

<!-- OUTPUT: free -h with both sessions running -->

## Recap

1. One open port can serve several services, including the app we could only reach through an SSH tunnel before. `nginx` listens on `80` and sends each path to a service that only listens on `127.0.0.1`.

2. Each service needs to know its path. RStudio Server learns it from the `X-RStudio-Root-Path` header, and JupyterHub learns it from `bind_url`. `baseball-trajectory` never needs to know, because `nginx` strips the prefix and Shiny's links are relative.

3. On AL2023, the `location` blocks go in `/etc/nginx/default.d/` and the WebSocket `map` goes in `/etc/nginx/conf.d/`, so `nginx.conf` stays untouched.

4. The new security group rule opens port `80` to our IP only, because plain HTTP sends passwords unencrypted. [Configure SSL](configure-ssl.qmd) adds HTTPS.
